Literal Interpretation

The Death of Sarah

Genesis 23 opens with the death of the matriarch Sarah, the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac. "And Sara lived a hundred and twenty-seven years. And she died in the city of Arbee which is Hebron, in the land of Chanaan: and Abraham came to mourn for Sara, and to weep for her" (Gen 23:1-2). Sarah is the only woman in Scripture whose age at death is explicitly recorded, an indication of her singular importance in salvation history.

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, reflects on the proper manner of Christian mourning, teaching that we should grieve with hope. In his homily on John's Gospel, he writes:

"I do not forbid weeping, but forbid the beating yourselves, the weeping immoderately... Weep, but gently, but with decency, but with the fear of God. If so you weep, you do so not as disbelieving the Resurrection, but as not enduring the separation."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of John, Homily 62

Abraham's mourning demonstrates the balance between natural grief and supernatural hope. He came "to mourn for Sara, and to weep for her," yet his subsequent actions show his faith in God's promises regarding the land and the resurrection.

Abraham the Stranger and Sojourner

After his period of mourning, Abraham rises and speaks to the sons of Heth (the Hittites), saying: "I am a stranger and a sojourner among you: give me the right of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead" (Gen 23:4). This self-description as a "stranger and sojourner" is deeply significant and is echoed throughout Scripture.

The Letter to the Hebrews interprets this confession in light of Abraham's heavenly hope:

"These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off were assured of them, embraced them and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things declare plainly that they seek a homeland... But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly country."

Hebrews 11:13-16

Abraham called himself a stranger not merely because he came from Ur of the Chaldeans, but because he recognized that his true home was in heaven. This confession of pilgrim status becomes a model for all believers who sojourn through this world awaiting their eternal inheritance.

The Negotiation with the Sons of Heth

The Hittites respond to Abraham with great respect: "Thou art a prince of God among us: bury thy dead in our principal sepulchres" (Gen 23:6). The Hebrew phrase nesi Elohim ("prince of God") indicates that Abraham's status as a man blessed by God was evident even to pagans.

Abraham bows to the people of the land and requests specifically the cave of Machpelah, which belongs to Ephron the Hittite. The name "Machpelah" means "double" in Hebrew, likely referring to the cave's double chambers or twin entrances. This cave, located at the end of Ephron's field near Mamre (Hebron), would become the burial place of the patriarchs.

The Purchase from Ephron

Ephron initially offers to give the field and cave to Abraham as a gift (Gen 23:11), but Abraham insists on paying full price. This negotiation follows ancient Near Eastern customs, where such offers might be polite formalities requiring refusal. Ephron finally names his price: "My lord, hear me: the ground which thou desirest, is worth four hundred sicles of silver: this is the price between me and thee" (Gen 23:15).

Four hundred shekels of silver was a substantial sum. For comparison, Jeremiah later purchased a field for only seventeen shekels (Jer 32:9). Abraham pays without bargaining, weighing out the silver "current money with the merchant" (Gen 23:16). This transaction represents the first recorded purchase of land and the first use of silver as a medium of exchange in Scripture.

The Legal Transfer

The text carefully records the legal transfer of property: "And the field was made sure to Abraham, and the cave that was in it, and all the trees that were in all the bounds thereof round about. So the field and the cave were assured to Abraham for a possession to bury in, by the sons of Heth" (Gen 23:17-18, 20). The detailed description of the property boundaries and the public nature of the transaction before the city gates served as legal documentation in a pre-literate society.

The Burial of Sarah

The chapter concludes simply: "And so Abraham buried Sara his wife, in a double cave of the field, that looked towards Mamre, this is Hebron in the land of Chanaan" (Gen 23:19). This cave would become the family tomb, where Abraham himself (Gen 25:9), Isaac and Rebekah (Gen 49:31), and Jacob and Leah (Gen 49:31) would all be buried.

The Cave of the Patriarchs, known today as the Ibrahimi Mosque or the Tomb of the Patriarchs in Hebron, remains one of the most ancient and continuously venerated sites in the Holy Land. The enclosure around the tombs is attributed to Herod the Great and represents the only fully intact Herodian structure surviving today.

Allegorical Interpretation

Sarah as Type of the Church

In the allegorical tradition established by St. Paul in Galatians 4, Sarah represents the New Covenant and the heavenly Jerusalem. Her death and burial, therefore, carry typological significance for understanding the Church and its relationship to the earthly and heavenly realms.

St. Augustine, in the City of God, develops the typology of Sarah as the free woman who bears the children of promise:

"Citizens are begotten to the earthly city by nature vitiated by sin, but to the heavenly city by grace freeing nature from sin; whence the former are called 'vessels of wrath,' the latter 'vessels of mercy.' This was typified in the two sons of Abraham: Ishmael, the son of Hagar the handmaid, being born according to the flesh, while Isaac was born of the free woman Sarah, according to the promise."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

Sarah's one hundred twenty-seven years of life span the entire narrative of Abraham's call and the birth of the promised seed. Her death marks the end of an era and the transition to the next generation of the covenant people, just as the earthly Church militant transitions to the Church triumphant.

The Cave of Machpelah as Type of Christ's Tomb

The purchased cave where Sarah was buried prefigures the tomb of Christ. Just as Abraham purchased a burial place for Sarah with silver, so Joseph of Arimathea provided his own new tomb for the burial of our Lord. Both were caves hewn from rock; both received the body of one through whom the promises would be fulfilled.

The name "Machpelah," meaning "double," has been interpreted allegorically to signify the dual nature of Christ (divine and human), the two covenants (old and new), or the twofold resurrection hope (of Christ and of His members). As Christ's tomb was both the place of burial and the site of resurrection, so the Cave of Machpelah, though a place of death, became the resting place of those who awaited the resurrection.

Abraham as Figure of God the Father

Medieval interpreters developed an allegory in which Abraham represents God the Father who purchases a dwelling place for His beloved. As Abraham paid the full price for the burial cave, so God "spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all" (Rom 8:32). The four hundred shekels of silver, a substantial and complete payment, prefigures the infinite price paid for human redemption.

"Abraham is understood as God the Father... The Church, established under grace, with the Christian people is enriched with the kingdom of God."

Medieval patristic interpretation

The Stranger and Sojourner

Abraham's confession that he was "a stranger and a sojourner" among the Hittites carries allegorical weight. The Church herself is a stranger and pilgrim in this world, possessing no permanent dwelling here but seeking the city that is to come (Heb 13:14).

St. Augustine explains how the earthly city and the heavenly city are intermingled in this present age:

"In Books XV-XVI, having treated the origin of the two cities (earthly and heavenly), Augustine explains their growth and progress. The progress of the heavenly city alone, from Abraham to the kings of Israel, shows how the pilgrim people of God sojourn through this world."

St. Augustine, City of God, Books XV-XVI

The faithful are called to live as strangers and pilgrims (1 Pet 2:11), recognizing that their citizenship is in heaven. Abraham's purchase of a burial plot, not a dwelling place, demonstrates that his expectations were fixed on the world to come.

The Field and Trees

The legal description of Abraham's purchase includes not only the cave but also "the field... and all the trees that were in all the bounds thereof" (Gen 23:17). Origen and the Alexandrian school found spiritual significance in such details:

"Observe each detail which has been written. For, if one knows how to dig into the depth, he will find a treasure in the details, and perhaps also, the precious jewels of the mysteries lie hidden where they are not esteemed."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The field may represent the world which Christ purchased with His blood; the trees, the faithful who are planted in the Lord's vineyard. The cave itself, hidden within the field, represents the mystery of death and resurrection concealed within the visible creation.

Sarah as Wisdom

Building on Philo's interpretation, some Fathers saw Sarah as a figure of divine Wisdom. Her name, meaning "princess" or "noblewoman," and her unique status as Abraham's half-sister and wife, suggested the intimate relationship between the faithful soul and divine Wisdom.

Origen drew from various traditions to illuminate the allegorical significance:

"Origen stated: 'I, following Paul the apostle, say that these things are allegories and I say that the marriages of the saints are the union of the soul with the word of God.'"

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The death of Sarah, then, might represent the soul's separation from earthly wisdom in order to attain heavenly wisdom, or the passing of the Old Covenant's understanding to make way for the fuller revelation in Christ.

The Sons of Heth

The Hittites, called "sons of Heth," represent the Gentile nations who would ultimately receive the children of Abraham into their midst. Their recognition of Abraham as "a prince of God" (Gen 23:6) prefigures the Gentiles' recognition of the God of Israel through the preaching of the Gospel.

St. Irenaeus emphasized the continuity of God's promises from Abraham to the Church:

"Those who disallow his salvation, and frame the idea of another God besides Him who made the promise to Abraham, are outside the kingdom of God, and are disinherited from the gift of incorruption, setting at naught and blaspheming God, who introduces, through Jesus Christ, Abraham to the kingdom of heaven, and his seed, that is, the Church."

St. Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses, Book IV

The Gentile Hittites who honored Abraham and sold him the burial cave become types of the Gentile believers who receive the Gospel and provide a place for the Church among the nations.
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

Christian Mourning: Grief Tempered by Hope

Abraham's response to Sarah's death provides a model for Christian mourning. He came "to mourn for Sara, and to weep for her" (Gen 23:2), acknowledging the natural grief of bereavement, yet his subsequent actions demonstrate faith and composure rather than despair.

St. Basil the Great counsels believers on how to grieve with Christian hope:

"It is God's command that we who trust in Christ should not grieve over them who are fallen asleep, because we hope in the resurrection; and that in reward for great patience great crowns of glory are kept in store by the Master of life's course."

St. Basil the Great, Letters

Basil further advises that in times of loss, we should bring out "sober reason which in our happy days is wont to draw lines of limitation round our souls, and when troubles come about us to recall to our minds that we are but men." The Christian neither suppresses grief nor surrenders to it, but grieves with the measured hope of resurrection.

St. Gregory of Nyssa, who lost his brother Basil and his sister Macrina, understood the struggle between grief and hope. After Macrina's death, he wrote:

"Macrina first allows Gregory to give expression to his grief: 'She, like an expert equestrian, allowed me briefly to be carried away by the torrent of my grief.' However, her patience with her brother does not last long: 'Then she endeavored to bridle me with words and to steer with the bit of her own reasoning the disorder of my soul. The apostolic saying put forward by her was: One ought not grieve for those who have fallen sleep, for this is the passion only of those who have no hope.'"

St. Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection

The Virtue of Honest Dealing

Abraham's negotiation with Ephron demonstrates exemplary honesty in business transactions. Though the Hittites offered him a burial place freely (Gen 23:6) and Ephron specifically offered the field as a gift (Gen 23:11), Abraham insisted on paying the full price publicly, before witnesses.

"Abraham does not argue or bargain with Ephron, but agrees to pay the full price without hesitation. He weighs out the silver and gives it to Ephron in the presence of the witnesses. He shows his faith and obedience to God, who had promised to give him and his descendants the land as an everlasting possession."

Traditional moral commentary

This teaches several moral lessons. First, Abraham avoided any appearance of impropriety by insisting on a legitimate purchase. Second, he dealt openly before witnesses, establishing clear title that could not later be disputed. Third, he paid generously without haggling, preferring to err on the side of generosity rather than risk taking advantage of the seller.

Pilgrimage and Detachment

Abraham's confession that he was "a stranger and a sojourner" (Gen 23:4) has profound moral implications. Though God had promised him the entire land of Canaan, Abraham lived his whole life without possessing it, except for this burial cave purchased with his own money.

St. Basil teaches that we should set eternal hope against present grief:

"Set expected joys over against present griefs, and thus thou wilt preserve for thyself that calm and quiet of the soul... Rise above the sensible perception of present things and fix thy mind on the hope of things eternal."

St. Basil the Great, Letters

This attitude of pilgrim detachment does not mean indifference to earthly responsibilities. Abraham still mourned his wife, still provided for her honorable burial, still conducted business with integrity. But his ultimate hope was fixed on the heavenly country, not on earthly possessions.

Honoring the Dead

The careful attention Abraham gives to Sarah's burial establishes the moral importance of honoring the dead. His willingness to pay a substantial sum for a proper burial place demonstrates that the bodies of the deceased deserve reverent treatment.

The Fathers consistently taught that Christian burial practices reflect our belief in the resurrection. Tertullian defended the Christian hope in bodily resurrection:

"The resurrection of the dead is the Christian's trust. By it we are believers... If God raises not men entire, he raises not the dead."

Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh

Abraham's care for Sarah's body, even after her death, reflects his faith that death is not the end. The body that housed the soul is still worthy of honor and will be raised in glory at the last day.

Prudence in Temporal Affairs

Though Abraham was a man of faith whose eyes were fixed on heaven, he conducted his earthly affairs with wisdom and prudence. He negotiated carefully, ensuring clear legal title. He chose a specific location for strategic reasons. He paid in "current money with the merchant," using proper commercial standards.

This demonstrates that spiritual-mindedness does not excuse carelessness in practical matters. The Christian is called to be wise as a serpent while innocent as a dove (Matt 10:16). Abraham's example shows that faithfulness to God includes faithful stewardship of temporal responsibilities.

Sarah as Model of Faith

The Apostle Peter holds up Sarah as a model for Christian women:

"Just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear."

1 Peter 3:6

Sarah's faith is also commemorated in the Letter to the Hebrews: "By faith also Sara herself, being barren, received strength to conceive seed, even past the time of age; because she judged him faithful who had promised" (Heb 11:11). Her death at one hundred twenty-seven years concluded a life of faith that made her the mother of all who believe.

The prophet Isaiah calls the righteous to look to Sarah as their spiritual mother:

"Look to Abraham, your father, and to Sarah who gave birth to you."

Isaiah 51:2

Perseverance to the End

Sarah's long life and faithful death remind us of the importance of persevering to the end. She waited decades for the fulfillment of God's promise, finally receiving Isaac in her old age. She lived to see her son grow to adulthood but died before seeing the full flowering of the covenant promises.

St. Basil encourages perseverance through trials:

"Play the man... the blow is a heavy one, but stand firm; do not fall under the weight of your grief; do not lose heart."

St. Basil the Great, Letters

Like Sarah, we may not see the complete fulfillment of God's promises in this life. But faith perseveres, trusting that God is faithful who promised, and that what He has begun He will bring to completion.
anagogical:
Anagogical Interpretation

The Resurrection Hope

Abraham's careful provision for Sarah's burial reflects his faith in the resurrection of the dead. The patriarchs' insistence on burial in the promised land expressed their confidence that God would fulfill His promises, including the promise of resurrection and eternal inheritance.

Modern scholarship on the Old Testament hope of resurrection notes:

"The patriarchs did not believe death would hinder the fulfillment of their promised inheritance... The care concerning the details of burial places look forward to the restoration and resurrection promised by God."

Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society, "The Genesis of Resurrection Hope"

The Letter to the Hebrews explicitly connects Abraham's faith to resurrection hope, noting that when Abraham was ready to sacrifice Isaac, "he considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back" (Heb 11:19). If Abraham believed God could raise Isaac from death, he surely believed God could raise Sarah as well.

The Cave as Waiting Place

The Cave of Machpelah, where the patriarchs and matriarchs were laid to rest, becomes an image of the state of the faithful dead who await the resurrection. They rest "in hope" (Ps 16:9), their bodies returning to dust but destined for glory.

Tertullian defended the Christian belief in bodily resurrection against those who spiritualized it away:

"All the material parts of self that have decayed, been cut off, swallowed and digested, and/or scattered in death will be reconstituted in the end. In Tertullian's words, from 'the maws of beasts, and the crops of birds' people's bodies will be 'rehabilitated from corruption to integrity.'"

Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh

The double chamber of Machpelah (the meaning of the name) may signify the two states of the faithful dead: the present rest of their souls with Christ, and the future resurrection of their bodies at His coming.

The Heavenly Country

Abraham's confession that he was a stranger and sojourner points beyond the promised land of Canaan to the heavenly homeland. The Letter to the Hebrews makes this eschatological meaning explicit:

"These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off were assured of them, embraced them and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things declare plainly that they seek a homeland... But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly country. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them."

Hebrews 11:13-16

St. Augustine extensively develops the theme of the heavenly city in contrast to the earthly:

"Two things are promised to Abraham: the one, that his seed should possess the land of Canaan, which is intimated when it is said, 'Go into a land that I will show you, and I will make of you a great nation'; but the other far more excellent, not about the carnal but the spiritual seed, through which he is the father, not of the one Israelite nation, but of all nations who follow the footprints of his faith."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

The earthly inheritance in Canaan was a type of the heavenly inheritance. Abraham possessed only a burial cave in this life, but he looked forward to the city "which has foundations, whose architect and builder is God" (Heb 11:10).

The Purchase Price and Redemption

Abraham's payment of four hundred shekels of silver for the burial cave may be seen as a type of the price of redemption. As Abraham paid the full price to secure a place for his beloved's body, so Christ paid the full price of His precious blood to secure eternal dwelling places for His beloved Church.

St. Irenaeus emphasizes that God's promises to Abraham find their fulfillment in Christ and the Church:

"God, who introduces, through Jesus Christ, Abraham to the kingdom of heaven, and his seed, that is, the Church, upon which also is conferred the adoption and the inheritance promised to Abraham."

St. Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses, Book IV

The inheritance promised to Abraham is not merely the land of Canaan but the new heavens and new earth, the eternal kingdom where the righteous will dwell forever.

Sarah's Rest and the Sabbath of Eternity

Sarah's death at one hundred twenty-seven years and her rest in the cave prefigure the eternal Sabbath rest that awaits the people of God. The Letter to the Hebrews teaches: "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God" (Heb 4:9).

St. Gregory of Nyssa, in his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, presents a hopeful vision of the final restoration:

"Gregory argues that when Paul says that God will be 'all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), this means that... eventually 'no being will remain outside the number of the saved' and that 'no being created by God will fall outside the Kingdom of God'... Christ's incarnation, death and resurrection results in 'total salvation for human nature.'"

St. Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection

Sarah's rest in the cave is temporary; she awaits the resurrection when, with all the faithful, she will enter into the eternal rest of God's presence.

The Tomb and the Temple

Jewish mystical tradition, as recorded in sources like the Midrash and Zohar, connected the Cave of Machpelah with paradise and the presence of God:

"The Zohar, the classic text of Jewish mysticism, relates that Abraham also witnessed the entrance to the Garden of Eden in the cave."

Traditional Jewish interpretation

While Christian interpretation does not depend on such traditions, they reflect an intuition that the burial place of the patriarchs is somehow connected to eternal life and the divine presence. The cave becomes a vestibule of heaven, a place where the faithful dead await the opening of paradise.

The New Jerusalem

The city of Hebron, where Sarah was buried, was later called Kiriath-arba ("city of four"). This city, associated with death and burial, contrasts with the heavenly Jerusalem that comes down from God, where "death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more" (Rev 21:4).

St. Augustine describes the destiny of those who, like Abraham, are citizens of the City of God:

"Sarah, the free woman, who prefigured the free city (which again was also prefigured in another way by that shadow of a city Jerusalem)... The children of promise are the citizens of the free city, the heavenly Jerusalem."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

The faithful who die in the Lord, like Sarah, are destined not for an earthly cave but for the heavenly city, the new Jerusalem, where they will dwell forever in the presence of God and the Lamb.

The Joy of Reunion

The separation caused by death is temporary for those who die in faith. Abraham's mourning for Sarah will give way to eternal reunion. The sorrow of parting will be transformed into the joy of the resurrection, when "your sorrow shall be turned into joy... and your joy no man shall take from you" (Jn 16:20-22).

St. John Chrysostom counsels Christians to view death as a temporary separation, not a final farewell:

"Since even over those who are leaving us, and departing to foreign lands, we weep, yet we do this not as despairing... And so do thou weep, as if you were sending one on his way to another land."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of John, Homily 62

Sarah has departed to another land, the heavenly country. Abraham will follow, as will all the faithful. And in the resurrection, they will be reunited forever in the presence of God, in that city where there is no more death, neither sorrow nor crying, but everlasting joy in the vision of the Holy Trinity.
